question:
Patient note:
A 40-year-old man with no known chronic cardiopulmonary, renal, hepatic, or hematologic illness was transported to the hospital’s medical intensive care admission bay after developing sudden epigastric pain radiating to the back while finishing a late shift at a printing warehouse, followed by several bouts of non-bloody, non-bilious emesis and a single episode of near-syncope in the break room. Coworkers reported that he had been complaining of vague upper-abdominal discomfort for two days and had taken only over-the-counter ibuprofen for what he thought was heartburn; he otherwise takes no prescription drugs, smokes fewer than three cigarettes a week, drinks beer socially on weekends, and denies illicit substances. He has never required hospitalization, systemic steroids, chemotherapy, biologic agents, or dialysis and his last employment physical twelve months earlier documented entirely normal bloodwork. Emergency medical technicians located him seated forward on a chair, clutching his mid-abdomen, diaphoretic but responsive, with portable pulse oximetry reading 88 % on ambient air; they applied a Venturi mask that the respiratory therapist later verified was delivering 40 % inspired oxygen, established a single 20-gauge peripheral line but infused no crystalloid, analgesic, antiemetic, antibiotic, or vasoactive medication during the nine-minute transport. On rolling into the resuscitation alcove—and prior to any hospital-initiated therapy—the admitting nurse obtained a first full set of vital signs: oral temperature 100.1 °F, non-invasive blood pressure 122/78 mm Hg corroborated manually, radial pulse 97 beats per minute in regular sinus rhythm, and a spontaneous respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute without accessory-muscle use. The patient was sitting upright, conversing in complete sentences, oriented to person, place, time, and circumstance, able to recall three objects after five minutes, and obeying complex commands, yielding a Glasgow Coma Scale of 15 with no sedatives, ethanol, or recreational drugs on board. His skin was warm and lightly diaphoretic; capillary refill was brisk, and there was no cyanosis or mottling. Sclerae were anicteric, mucous membranes moist, and jugular venous pulsations were not elevated at 30 degrees. Cardiac auscultation revealed a crisp S1 and single physiologic S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs; distal pulses were 2+ and symmetric. Lungs were clear to percussion; breath sounds were mildly diminished at both bases but free of crackles, wheezes, or rubs. Abdominal examination disclosed a soft yet exquisitely tender epigastrium with voluntary guarding and hypoactive bowel sounds but no rebound, distension, or organomegaly. There was no costovertebral angle tenderness. Extremities were warm and without edema; neurologic screening showed intact strength, sensation, and reflexes throughout. Within ten minutes of stretcher placement, a radial arterial sample drawn while he remained on the 40 % mask demonstrated a pH of 7.34, PaCO₂ 38 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 66 mm Hg, indicating mild hypoxemia relative to delivered oxygen fraction with near-normal acid–base status. Serum chemistry obtained from the same stick showed sodium 142 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, glucose 109 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, the latter matching his prior occupational screen and arguing against renal impairment. A complete blood count returned white blood cell count 11 000 / mm³ with 76 % neutrophils, hematocrit 43 %, hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, and platelets 245 000 / µL. Serum lipase drawn concurrently was markedly elevated at 2 480 U/L, and triglycerides measured 215 mg/dL; alcohol level was undetectable. Point-of-care lactate was 1.6 mmol/L. An upright abdominal radiograph obtained before any narcotic or antiemetic therapy revealed a sentinel loop in the left upper quadrant with no free air; a portable anteroposterior chest film showed clear lung fields, normal cardiac silhouette, and a small left-sided pleural effusion but no infiltrate or pneumothorax. Electrocardiography performed fifteen minutes after arrival demonstrated sinus rhythm at 95 beats per minute with normal intervals and no ST-segment deviation. Focused cardiac ultrasound revealed a normally contracting left ventricle without pericardial effusion, and inferior vena cava diameter varied appropriately with respiration. Foley catheterization in triage yielded 120 mL of clear yellow urine. Importantly, during the approximately thirty-five minutes between ambulance arrival and handoff to the ICU team he received no intravenous fluids, antibiotics, opioids, sedatives, proton-pump inhibitors, steroids, or vasopressors; therefore the physiologic and laboratory values—temperature 100.1 °F, systolic pressure 122 mm Hg, diastolic pressure 78 mm Hg, heart rate 97 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, arterial pH 7.34, serum sodium 142 mmol/L, serum potassium 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, hematocrit 43 %, white blood cell count 11 000 / mm³, fraction of inspired oxygen 40 %, and arterial oxygen tension 66 mm Hg—represent his untreated presentation at the moment of intensive care admission for presumed acute gallstone pancreatitis complicated by early hypoxemic respiratory compromise.

Question: What is the patient's APACHE II score?
solution:
APACHE II adds acute physiology points, age points, and points for severe chronic organ insufficiency or immunocompromise. Using the supplied admission values:
- Temperature 100.1 °F (37.8 °C): 0; mean arterial pressure (122 + 2 × 78)/3 ≈ 93 mm Hg: 0; heart rate 97/min: 0; respiratory rate 20/min: 0.
- Oxygenation: FiO₂ is 0.40 (<0.50), so use PaO₂ rather than the alveolar–arterial gradient. PaO₂ 66 mm Hg falls in the 61–70 range: 1.
- Arterial pH 7.34: 0; sodium 142 mmol/L: 0; potassium 4.1 mmol/L: 0; creatinine 0.8 mg/dL: 0.
- Hematocrit 43%: 0; WBC 11,000/mm³: 0; neurologic points = 15 − GCS 15 = 0.
- Age 40 (<45): 0. No qualifying chronic organ insufficiency or immunocompromise: 0.
Total = 1 acute physiology point + 0 age + 0 chronic health = 1.
Final answer: 1
